subject: estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model

messages.author: 7b2fb40653accdcf
messages.subject: estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
parts:
Hello,

I'm working on a project to estimate the variability of "growth" measures in education, specifically the Colorado model, which uses quantile regression to estimate the conditional distribution of the most current test results for a student given between 1 and 4 years of prior test scores.  The growth score is presented as a point estimate with no indication of its variability.

I want to use a Bayesian model with an IRT model with known parameters as the data generating process to estimate the conditional distribution of the most recent score given the scores from previous years, and using it to compute the "growth" score and its variability, where the "growth" score is defined as 100 times the sum of the conditional probabilities of all possible scores that are lower than the student's actual score. 

I have a STAN model that seems to work pretty well with two years of data and I'm interested in any suggestions on how to go about incorporating more than two years of data.  Each year will have a different IRT model, and I'd like to tie them together to get a single posterior predictive distribution for the most current year.

In the two year case, I did this by providing only a single ability parameter value for each student that applies to both years (I'm using a 1PL model and the difficulty values vary from year to year).  I'm wondering if there is a better way to do this.

Best regards,

Gene Quinn

code is on github https://github.com/equinn1/STAN.   growth.pdf contains background information on the project.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
parts:
What we'd probably do is treat the student abilities in the IRT
model as a time series then give everything a multilevel prior.

So something like for your model, generalize theta to allow
it to vary by year,

vector[N_year] theta[N_stu];

then take a multivariate prior (as described in the manual
regression chapter), so that

for (n in 1:N_stu)
theta[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(...);

That is, there's a multivariate normal prior on a student's abilities
across years.

- Bob

messages.author: 7b2fb40653accdcf
messages.subject: Re: estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
parts:
Just a quick followup:

After realizing how difficult the prediction problem is, I decided to retreat a simpler problem.  Given the ability parameter theta in the IRT model, the conditional distribution of scores for the student should be determined independently of any previous test results.  "Growth" can be calculated from this conditional distribution as 100*F(x-1) where F is the conditional CDF.  The Colorado model attempts to determine this approximately with quantile regression. 

So I did two simulations with STAN,
1)  Use a betabinomial model and compute the "growth" from the (analytic) posteriors
2)  Construct a STAN model corresponding to the MCAS, which is a mixture of 2PL, 3PL, and polytomous items, using informative normal priors for the IRT parameters (the standardization process produces estimates of the mean and standard deviation of each parameter).  Generate scaled scores and use their sampling distribution to estimate 100*F(x-1) for each possible score.

I used the samples generated from the betabinomial as input to the SGP package, and found that the SGP results generally match  the theoretical value of 100*F(x-1).  I was also able to compute expected values, standard deviations, and credible intervals for "growth".
